claim: The parabrachial nucleus (PBN) is a major hub that receives sensory information from both internal and external environments.
source: The parabrachial nucleus (PBN) is a major hub that receives sensory information from both internal and external environments.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that characterizes the PBN's role based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Specific populations of PBN neurons are involved in behaviors including food and water intake, nociceptive responses, breathing regulation, as well as learning and responding appropriately to threatening stimuli.
source: Specific populations of PBN neurons are involved in behaviors including food and water intake, nociceptive responses, breathing regulation, as well as learning and responding appropriately to threatening stimuli.
evidence: This statement in the abstract summarizes known functions of PBN neurons based on prior research.

claim: Using single-cell RNA sequencing, 21 subclusters of neurons in the PBN and neighboring regions were identified.
source: Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we identified 21 subclusters of neurons in the PBN and neighboring regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the scRNA-Seq experiment reported in the manuscript.

claim: Multiplexed in situ hybridization showed many of these subclusters are enriched within specific PBN subregions with scattered cells in several other regions.
source: Multiplexed in situ hybridization showed many of these subclusters are enriched within specific PBN subregions with scattered cells in several other regions.
evidence: This finding is based on HiPlex in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Detailed visualization of the axonal projections from 21 Cre-driver lines of mice was provided.
source: We also provide detailed visualization of the axonal projections from 21 Cre-driver lines of mice.
evidence: This describes the viral tracing experiments conducted in the study.

claim: The PBN is located at the junction of the midbrain and pons.
source: The parabrachial nucleus (PBN), located at the junction of the midbrain and pons, relays sensory information from the periphery primarily to the forebrain, thereby playing a major role in informing the brain of both the internal state (interoception) and external conditions (exteroception) to facilitate responses to adverse conditions and help maintain homeostasis.
evidence: This is an anatomical description based on established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: The PBN relays sensory information from the periphery primarily to the forebrain.
source: The parabrachial nucleus (PBN), located at the junction of the midbrain and pons, relays sensory information from the periphery primarily to the forebrain, thereby playing a major role in informing the brain of both the internal state (interoception) and external conditions (exteroception) to facilitate responses to adverse conditions and help maintain homeostasis.
evidence: This describes the functional role of the PBN based on established knowledge.

claim: The earliest reference to the PBN was from Herrick, 1905, who implicated it in transmitting gustatory signals.
source: The earliest reference to the PBN was from Herrick, 1905, who implicated it in transmitting gustatory signals and later elaborated upon by Norgren and Leonard, 1971.
evidence: This is a historical reference citing prior work.

claim: The inputs and outputs of the PBN have been studied extensively using anterograde and retrograde methods.
source: The inputs and outputs of the PBN have been studied extensively using anterograde and retrograde methods (Fulwiler and Saper, 1984; Gauriau and Bernard, 2002; Krout and Loewy, 2000; Moga et al., 1990; Norgren, 1976; Saper and Loewy, 1980; Tokita et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement references multiple prior studies that characterized PBN connectivity.

claim: The vagus transmits signals from internal organs, including the gastrointestinal system, to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), which then projects to the PBN.
source: The vagus transmits signals from internal organs, including the gastrointestinal system, to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), which then projects to the PBN; thus, detection of visceral signals related to food and malaise depends on this circuit.
evidence: This describes a known neural circuit based on established neuroanatomy.

claim: Detection of visceral signals related to food and malaise depends on the vagus-NTS-PBN circuit.
source: The vagus transmits signals from internal organs, including the gastrointestinal system, to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), which then projects to the PBN; thus, detection of visceral signals related to food and malaise depends on this circuit.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional role of the circuit based on its anatomy.

claim: Other internal organs, muscle, and bone transmit nociceptive signals via intermediary ganglia to the spinal cord and then directly to the PBN.
source: Other internal organs, muscle, and bone transmit nociceptive signals via intermediary ganglia to the spinal cord and then directly to the PBN.
evidence: This describes known sensory pathways to the PBN.

claim: Ascending fibers from the spinal cord relay peripheral temperature and pain signals directly to the PBN.
source: Ascending fibers from the spinal cord relay peripheral temperature and pain signals directly to the PBN, while trigeminal neurons relay these signals from the face.
evidence: This describes known sensory pathways based on established neuroanatomy.

claim: Trigeminal neurons relay temperature and pain signals from the face to the PBN.
source: Ascending fibers from the spinal cord relay peripheral temperature and pain signals directly to the PBN, while trigeminal neurons relay these signals from the face.
evidence: This describes a known sensory pathway.

claim: Blood-borne threats to homeostasis are detected by the area postrema and transmitted to the PBN.
source: In addition, blood-borne threats to homeostasis are detected by the area postrema and transmitted to the PBN (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement cites a specific study describing this pathway.

claim: Taste is transmitted from the tongue and palate via branches of the facial, petrosal, glossopharyngeal nerves to the rostral NTS and from there to the PBN.
source: Taste is transmitted from the tongue and palate via branches of the facial, petrosal, glossopharyngeal nerves to the rostral NTS and from there to the PBN.
evidence: This describes the known gustatory pathway to the PBN.

claim: Calcium imaging and Fos-induction studies show that most sensory systems can activate neurons in the PBN.
source: Additionally, calcium imaging and Fos-induction studies show that most sensory systems can activate neurons in the PBN (Campos et al., 2018; Carter et al., 2013; Kang et al., 2022), although the neuronal circuits involved are not well established.
evidence: This statement cites multiple studies that used calcium imaging and Fos-induction to demonstrate PBN activation.

claim: Most afferent signals to the PBN are excitatory (glutamatergic).
source: Most of these afferent signals to the PBN are excitatory (glutamatergic), but there are also inhibitory, GABAergic inputs including those from the arcuate nucleus, bed nucleus of stria terminalis (BNST), and central nucleus of the amygdala (CEA).
evidence: This characterizes the neurotransmitter phenotype of PBN inputs based on established knowledge.

claim: There are inhibitory, GABAergic inputs to the PBN from the arcuate nucleus, bed nucleus of stria terminalis (BNST), and central nucleus of the amygdala (CEA).
source: Most of these afferent signals to the PBN are excitatory (glutamatergic), but there are also inhibitory, GABAergic inputs including those from the arcuate nucleus, bed nucleus of stria terminalis (BNST), and central nucleus of the amygdala (CEA).
evidence: This describes known inhibitory inputs to the PBN.

claim: The PBN projects axons to the periaqueductal gray (PAG), extended amygdala (including the BNST, CEA, substantia innominata, SI), the cerebral cortex (primarily the insular cortex), thalamus, parasubthalamic nucleus (PSTN), hypothalamus, and medulla.
source: The PBN projects axons to the periaqueductal gray (PAG), extended amygdala (including the BNST, CEA, substantia innominata, SI), the cerebral cortex (primarily the insular cortex), thalamus, parasubthalamic nucleus (PSTN), hypothalamus, and medulla.
evidence: This describes the known output targets of the PBN based on established neuroanatomy.

claim: The PBN is important for responding to internal and external stimuli and maintaining homeostasis.
source: Pioneering neuroanatomical studies encouraged functional studies (lesions, pharmacological and viral/genetic interventions), which have substantiated the predictions that the PBN is important for responding to internal and external stimuli and maintaining homeostasis.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on multiple functional studies.

claim: The PBN is involved in taste, thermal sensation, visceral malaise, pain, itch, hypercapnia, breathing, cardiovascular control, arousal, hunger/satiety, thirst, sodium appetite, and alarm.
source: Examples include taste, thermal sensation, visceral malaise, pain, itch, hypercapnia, breathing, cardiovascular control, arousal, hunger/satiety, thirst, sodium appetite, and alarm (Palmiter, 2018).
evidence: This statement cites a review that summarizes the diverse functions of the PBN.

claim: The PBN is bisected by a fiber tract, the superior cerebellar peduncle (scp), resulting in subregions that are lateral or medial to the scp in primates.
source: The PBN is bisected by a fiber tract, the superior cerebellar peduncle (scp), resulting in subregions that are lateral or medial to the scp in primates.
evidence: This describes the anatomical organization of the PBN based on established neuroanatomy.

claim: In rodents, the scp is rotated relative to that in primates such that so-called lateral regions are more dorsal to the scp, and medial regions are more ventral.
source: In rodents, the scp is rotated relative to that in primates such that so-called lateral regions are more dorsal to the scp, and medial regions are more ventral.
evidence: This describes the species-specific anatomical organization of the PBN.

claim: The ventral spinocerebellar tract (sctv) helps to define the dorsal border of the PBN in its caudal regions.
source: Another fiber pathway, the ventral spinocerebellar tract (sctv), helps to define the dorsal border of the PBN in its caudal regions.
evidence: This describes an anatomical landmark used to define PBN boundaries.

claim: The Kölliker-Fuse (KF) region, cuneiform nucleus, nucleus of the lateral lemniscus (NLL), mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus (MEV), and locus coeruleus (LC) are adjacent to the PBN.
source: The Kölliker-Fuse (KF) region (considered by some as part of the PBN), cuneiform nucleus, nucleus of the lateral lemniscus (NLL), mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus (MEV), and locus coeruleus (LC) are adjacent to it (Dong, 2008; Fulwiler and Saper, 1984; Paxinos and Franklin, 2019).
evidence: This describes the anatomical location of the PBN relative to neighboring structures, citing atlases.

claim: In situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry studies have revealed that the PBN is primarily glutamatergic and expresses an abundance of different neuropeptides and neuropeptide receptors.
source: In situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry studies have revealed that the PBN is primarily glutamatergic and expresses an abundance of different neuropeptides and neuropeptide receptors.
evidence: This summarizes findings from prior molecular characterization studies of the PBN.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed 13 transcript-defined glutamatergic neuron types within the PBN proper along with sparsely interspersed GABAergic neurons.
source: To define PBN cell types and gain insight into unique expression of signaling molecules and receptors, we adopted the single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-Seq) approach (Hashikawa et al., 2020; Macosko et al., 2015), which revealed 13 transcript-defined glutamatergic neuron types within the PBN proper along with sparsely interspersed GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the scRNA-Seq analysis.

claim: Brain tissue was harvested from 10 adult male and female C57BL/6J mice for scRNA-Seq.
source: To classify cell types in the mouse PBN according to their transcriptional profiles, we harvested brain tissue from 10 adult male and female C57BL/6J mice, excised the PBN along its rostral-caudal extension (Figure 1A), and prepared single-cell suspensions for high-throughput scRNA-Seq using a commercial droplet-based assay (10× Genomics).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for the scRNA-Seq experiment.

claim: After preprocessing, a total of 39,649 single-cell barcodes were retained that were sequenced to a median depth of 47,177 reads per cell.
source: After preprocessing the data to remove low-quality cells from the analysis (Rossi et al., 2021; Stuart et al., 2019), we retained a total of 39,649 single-cell barcodes that were sequenced to a median depth of 47,177 reads per cell.
evidence: This describes the quality and depth of the scRNA-Seq data.

claim: A total of 17,038 genes were detected, with a median of 1740 genes per cell.
source: A total of 17,038 genes were detected, with a median of 1740 genes per cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the gene detection statistics from the scRNA-Seq experiment, with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Low-resolution clustering identified seven transcriptionally distinct populations of neurons, glia, and stromal cells within the PBN.
source: Low-resolution clustering identified seven transcriptionally distinct populations of neurons, glia, and stromal cells within the PBN (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: This describes the initial clustering results from the scRNA-Seq analysis, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Neurons represented the largest proportion of cells at 57.2%.
source: Of these, neurons represented the largest proportion of cells at 57.2% (Figure 1C).
evidence: This quantifies the proportion of neurons in the dataset, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Oligodendrocytes, marked by Mag and Opalin, were detected at 24.1% of total cells.
source: Oligodendrocytes, marked by Mag and Opalin, were detected at 24.1% of total cells, and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs, 4.3% of total cells), were distinguished by their expression of Pdgfra and Gpr17 (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This quantifies oligodendrocytes and identifies their marker genes, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) represented 4.3% of total cells and were distinguished by their expression of Pdgfra and Gpr17.
source: Oligodendrocytes, marked by Mag and Opalin, were detected at 24.1% of total cells, and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs, 4.3% of total cells), were distinguished by their expression of Pdgfra and Gpr17 (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This quantifies OPCs and identifies their marker genes.

claim: The large number of oligodendrocytes and precursors is not surprising because the PBN is bisected by the scp.
source: The large number of oligodendrocytes and precursors is not surprising because the PBN is bisected by the scp.
evidence: This is an inference explaining the high proportion of oligodendrocytes based on the anatomical structure of the PBN.

claim: A population of astrocytes representing 8.1% of cells was detected that were labeled by robust expression of Agt and Slc4a4.
source: We detected a population of astrocytes representing 8.1% of cells that were labeled by robust expression of Agt and Slc4a4, as well as a smaller population of microglia (2.6%) that were specifically labeled by Cx3cr1 and Tmem119 (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This quantifies astrocytes and identifies their marker genes.

claim: A smaller population of microglia (2.6%) was specifically labeled by Cx3cr1 and Tmem119.
source: We detected a population of astrocytes representing 8.1% of cells that were labeled by robust expression of Agt and Slc4a4, as well as a smaller population of microglia (2.6%) that were specifically labeled by Cx3cr1 and Tmem119 (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This quantifies microglia and identifies their marker genes.

claim: Two distinct populations of stromal cells were identified; one characterized by selective expression of Tagln and Acta2 (3.2%), and another rare population of vascular leptomeningeal cells marked by Dcn and Slc6a13 (0.26% of total cells).
source: Additionally, we identified two distinct populations of cells marked by stromal markers; one of these populations was characterized by its selective expression of Tagln and Acta2 (3.2%), while another rare population of vascular leptomeningeal cells was marked by Dcn and Slc6a13 (0.26% of total cells).
evidence: This identifies and quantifies two stromal cell populations with their marker genes.

claim: Each cellular class was marked by a robust profile of unique transcriptional features.
source: Although known canonical markers were used for the biased identification of broad classes of resident cells within PBN tissue (Figure 1B and D), each of these cellular classes was marked by a robust profile of unique transcriptional features (Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the transcriptional characterization of cell types, with reference to Figure 1E and supplementary data.

claim: High-resolution subclustering of PBN neurons resulted in 7635 neurons sequenced to a median of 99,583 reads per cell with each cell containing a median of 3189 genes and 7823 transcripts.
source: To enable high-resolution subclustering of PBN neurons, we first applied a more stringent quality threshold to the neuronal population isolated in the initial analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E), resulting in a smaller set comprised 7635 neurons (Figure 2A–B). These cells were sequenced to a much higher median of 99,583 reads per cell with each cell containing a median of 3189 genes and 7823 transcripts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–O).
evidence: This describes the quality metrics for the high-resolution neuronal analysis.

claim: 21 unique subclusters of neurons (N1-N21) were discriminated according to their expression of differential feature sets.
source: We used a clustering approach like that applied for all cells and discriminated 21 unique subclusters of neurons (N1-N21) according to their expression of differential feature sets (Materials and methods, Figure 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1P–Q).
evidence: This describes the primary result of the high-resolution neuronal clustering.

claim: N1-N19 were designated as glutamatergic with N1, N2 being enriched in vesicular transporter Slc17a7 (Vglut1), while N3-N19 are enriched in vesicular transporter Slc17a6 (Vglut2).
source: We first classified neuronal subclusters as glutamatergic or GABAergic and designated N1-N19 as glutamatergic with N1, N2 being enriched in vesicular transporter Slc17a7 (Vglut1), while N3-N19 are enriched in vesicular transporter Slc17a6 (Vglut2); the latter account for about 90% of all neurons sequenced (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This classifies neuronal subclusters by neurotransmitter phenotype based on vesicular transporter expression.

claim: Slc17a6-expressing neurons account for about 90% of all neurons sequenced.
source: We first classified neuronal subclusters as glutamatergic or GABAergic and designated N1-N19 as glutamatergic with N1, N2 being enriched in vesicular transporter Slc17a7 (Vglut1), while N3-N19 are enriched in vesicular transporter Slc17a6 (Vglut2); the latter account for about 90% of all neurons sequenced (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This quantifies the proportion of Vglut2-expressing neurons.

claim: The remaining two subclusters N20, 21 are GABAergic based on expression of Gad1, Gad2, and Slc32a1 (Vgat).
source: The remaining two subclusters N20, 21 are GABAergic based on expression of Gad1, Gad2, and Slc32a1 (Vgat) (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This classifies two subclusters as GABAergic based on marker gene expression.

claim: Two major clades of neurons were identified that could be distinguished by their expression of transcription factors.
source: We sought to further define these 21 neuronal subclusters and identified two major clades that could be distinguished by their expression of transcription factors (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This describes a higher-order organization of neuronal subclusters based on transcription factor expression.

claim: One major clade (N4-N12) is represented by expression of Lhx2, Lhx9, Meis2, and Nrf1.
source: One major clade (N4-N12) is represented by expression of Lhx2, Lhx9, Meis2, and Nrf1.
evidence: This identifies transcription factors that characterize one major neuronal clade.

claim: The N4-N12 clade probably descends from neurons that express Atoh1 during development.
source: This clade probably descends from neurons that express Atoh1 during development (Karthik et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference about developmental origin based on a cited study.

claim: Another major clade that includes N13-N18 is represented by expression of homeobox-containing transcription factors Lmx1a, Lmx1b, Pou2f2, Pou6f2, En1, Tlx3, Onecut2, and Satb2, along with Rorb, Tfap2b, and Tle4.
source: Another major clade that includes N13-N18 (Figure 2F–G) is represented by expression of a group of homeobox-containing transcription factors Lmx1a, Lmx1b, Pou2f2, Pou6f2, En1, Tlx3, Onecut2, and Satb2, along with a member of the retinoic acid family (Rorb), the AP2 factor (Tfap2b), and co-repressor (Tle4).
evidence: This identifies transcription factors that characterize the second major neuronal clade.

claim: The two major clades represented by Atoh1 (N4-N12) and Lmx1 (N13-N18) descendants are largely non-overlapping populations.
source: The two major clades represented by Atoh1 (N4-N12) and Lmx1 (N13-N18) descendants are largely non-overlapping populations (Karthik et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the relationship between the two major clades, citing a reference.

claim: The Atoh1 clade follows a ventral pathway (VP) to the forebrain and the Lmx1 clade follows the central tegmental tract (CTT).
source: They have distinct axonal projection patterns, with the Atoh1 clade following a VP to the forebrain and the Lmx1 clade following the central tegmental tract (CTT).
evidence: This describes the distinct projection patterns of the two major clades.

claim: The two neuron subclusters that express Slc17a7 (N1 and N2) have distinct expression of transcription factors from each other and from the two major clades.
source: The two neuron subclusters that express Slc17a7 (N1 and N2) have distinct expression of transcription factors from each other and from the two major clades.
evidence: This describes the transcriptional distinctiveness of N1 and N2.

claim: The two subclusters that express Slc32a1 (N20, N21) also express distinct sets of transcription factors.
source: Likewise, the two subclusters that express Slc32a1 (N20, N21) also express distinct sets of transcription factors.
evidence: This describes the transcriptional distinctiveness of the GABAergic subclusters.

claim: The two major clades (N4-N12 and N13-N18) represent neurons that reside within the PBN.
source: As will be shown below, the two major clades (N4-N12 and N13-N18) represent neurons that reside within the PBN.
evidence: This is a statement about the anatomical location of the major clades, to be supported by subsequent data.

claim: The remaining two subclusters contain cells that mostly border the PBN and express Phox2b (N19) or Nfib and Lhx2 (N3).
source: The remaining two subclusters contain cells that mostly border the PBN and express Phox2b (N19) or Nfib and Lhx2 (N3) (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This describes the location and marker genes of subclusters outside the PBN proper.

claim: The 21 neuronal subclusters could be further delineated based on preferential expression of specific genes.
source: Within these two major clades, we also found that the 21 neuronal subclusters could be further delineated based on preferential expression of specific genes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes additional molecular characterization of the subclusters, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: This analysis identified multiple known subclasses of PBN neurons as well as novel neuronal subclusters and their corresponding transcriptional markers.
source: Although our analysis identified multiple known subclasses of PBN neurons, we also identified novel neuronal subclusters and their corresponding transcriptional markers.
evidence: This summarizes the novelty of the findings, identifying both known and new neuronal populations.

claim: This analysis provides a representation of PBN neuronal diversity at a higher resolution than has been previously appreciated.
source: Thus, this analysis provides a representation of PBN neuronal diversity at a higher resolution than has been previously appreciated (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: Some neuropeptide mRNAs are robustly expressed in one or two subclusters, e.g., Calca, Ghrh, Nps, Npy, Pdyn, Pnoc.
source: Some of these neuropeptide mRNAs are robustly expressed in one or two subclusters, e.g., Calca, Ghrh, Nps, Npy, Pdyn, Pnoc, while others are expressed in multiple subclusters, e.g., Adcyap1, Cck, Crh, Gal, Gpr, Nmb, Nts, Penk, Tac1, Vgf (Table 1, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This describes the expression patterns of neuropeptide genes across subclusters.

claim: Other neuropeptide mRNAs are expressed in multiple subclusters, e.g., Adcyap1, Cck, Crh, Gal, Gpr, Nmb, Nts, Penk, Tac1, Vgf.
source: Some of these neuropeptide mRNAs are robustly expressed in one or two subclusters, e.g., Calca, Ghrh, Nps, Npy, Pdyn, Pnoc, while others are expressed in multiple subclusters, e.g., Adcyap1, Cck, Crh, Gal, Gpr, Nmb, Nts, Penk, Tac1, Vgf (Table 1, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This describes the broader expression patterns of other neuropeptide genes.

claim: G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) genes are genetically useful because they are likely to be expressed in neurons that receive aminergic or neuropeptide input.
source: Like the neuropeptide group, the genes encoding G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are genetically useful because they are likely to be expressed in neurons that receive aminergic or neuropeptide input; thus, making them desirable for circuit mapping (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of GPCR genes for circuit mapping based on their functional role.

claim: GPCRs are viable targets for drugs that could potentially modify the function of select neurons and circuitry in the PBN.
source: GPCRs are also of interest because they are viable targets for drugs that could potentially modify the function of select neurons and circuitry in the PBN.
evidence: This is a statement about the therapeutic potential of targeting GPCRs.

claim: The expression of GPCR genes is generally much lower than that of neuropeptides, making them more difficult to detect by immunohistochemistry or in situ hybridization.
source: The expression of GPCR genes is generally much lower than that of neuropeptides, making them more difficult to detect by immunohistochemistry or in situ hybridization.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical challenges of detecting GPCR expression.

claim: scRNA-Seq data provide a resource for identifying the GPCRs expressed by distinct PBN neurons.
source: Consequently, scRNA-Seq data provide another resource for identifying the GPCRs expressed by distinct PBN neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of scRNA-Seq for GPCR detection.

claim: Fluorescent in situ hybridization was performed on coronal sections of the PBN spanning the rostral-caudal axis from Bregma –5.0 to –5.4 mm.
source: To determine if different neuron subclusters are in distinct PBN subdivisions, we performed fluorescent in situ hybridization on coronal sections of the PBN spanning the rostral-caudal axis from Bregma –5.0 to –5.4 mm.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach for anatomical localization of subclusters.

claim: Representative probes for each neuronal subcluster (N1-N21) were chosen based on the distinguishing genes in each subcluster.
source: Representative probes for each neuronal subcluster (N1-N21) were chosen based on the distinguishing genes in each subcluster (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the probe selection strategy for in situ hybridization.

claim: A composite image locating each subcluster within the PBN was generated based on the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas (AMBA) as a guide.
source: Two sets of 12 probes were used in HiPlex experiments and a composite image locating each subcluster within the PBN was generated based on the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas (AMBA) (Dong, 2008; Lein et al., 2007) as a guide (Figure 4B).
evidence: This describes the use of AMBA for anatomical reference in the HiPlex analysis.

claim: Only 13 glutamatergic of the 19 glutamatergic UMAP subclusters are within the PBN.
source: The tissue punch for scRNA-Seq was centered on the PBN, but neighboring regions were also included; consequently, only 13 glutamatergic of the 19 glutamatergic UMAP subclusters are within the PBN (Figure 4C).
evidence: This describes which subclusters are anatomically located within the PBN proper.

claim: PowerPoint summaries and individual TIFF images of all the HiPlex probes for the 5 Bregma levels of the PBN examined are available at Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.6707404).
source: PowerPoint summaries and individual TIFF images of all the HiPlex probes for the 5 Bregma levels of the PBN examined are available at Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.6707404).
evidence: This describes the public availability of the HiPlex data.

claim: Qualitative scoring of the expression of each probe within a specific PBN subregion is based on the number of transcripts (signal intensity) and number of cells.
source: Qualitative scoring of the expression of each probe within a specific PBN subregion (Figure 5A) or neighboring regions (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2) is based on the number of transcripts (signal intensity) and number of cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This describes the methodology for evaluating gene expression in the HiPlex data.

claim: The HiPlex data were supplemented with RNAScope experiments to further investigate differential gene expression within specific subclusters.
source: The HiPlex data were supplemented with RNAScope experiments to further investigate differential gene expression within specific subclusters.
evidence: This describes the use of additional in situ hybridization experiments to validate findings.

claim: Of the neuron subclusters identified by scRNA-Seq, some are in brain regions adjacent to the PBN (N1-3), some could not be identified (N5, 6, and 18), and the GABAergic cells are sparsely scattered throughout the PBN (N20, 21).
source: In summary, of the neuron subclusters identified by scRNA-Seq, some are in brain regions adjacent to the PBN (N1-3), some could not be identified (N5, 6, and 18), and the GABAergic cells are sparsely scattered throughout the PBN (N20, 21).
evidence: This is a summary of the anatomical localization results.

claim: 13 distinct clusters of excitatory neurons (N4, 7–17, and 19) are expressed within the PBN.
source: That leaves 13 distinct clusters of excitatory neurons (N4, 7–17, and 19) that are expressed within the PBN (Figure 4C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and 2).
evidence: This quantifies the number of glutamatergic subclusters within the PBN proper.

claim: Each of these PBN subclusters typically has prominent expression of the distinguishing genes in one subregion with less frequent expression in other subregions.
source: Each of these PBN subclusters typically has prominent expression of the distinguishing genes in one subregion with less frequent expression in other subregions.
evidence: This describes the general pattern of gene expression across PBN subregions.

claim: AAV1-Ef1a-DIO-YFP and AAV1-Ef1a-DIO-synaptophysin:mCherry were injected into the PBN of 21 Cre-driver lines to visualize cell bodies and processes within the PBN (YFP) and synapses (mCherry) throughout the entire brain.
source: We injected AAV1-Ef1a-DIO-YFP and AAV1-Ef1a-DIO-synaptophysin:mCherry into the PBN of 21 Cre-driver lines to visualize cell bodies and processes within the PBN (YFP) and synapses (mCherry) throughout the entire brain.
evidence: This describes the viral tracing methodology used to map projections.

claim: The viruses were bilaterally injected into PBN of four to five mice per Cre-driver line.
source: The viruses were bilaterally injected into PBN of four to five mice; after at least 3 weeks for viral expression, the mice were perfused for histology, and a preliminary analysis of viral expression in the PBN region was performed.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for the projection mapping experiments.

claim: Brains with the most precise viral placement were used to generate the TIFF stacks of the entire brain, available on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.6707404).
source: Brains with the most precise viral placement were used to generate the TIFF stacks of the entire brain, available on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.6707404).
evidence: This describes the data selection and public availability of projection data.

claim: The location(s) of fluorescent cell bodies in the PBN of the Cre-driver lines of mice is consistent with in situ hybridization results.
source: As expected, the location(s) of fluorescent cell bodies in the PBN of the Cre-driver lines of mice is consistent with in situ hybridization results, although the promoter in the virus and multiple viral particles per cell can provide more robust expression than the endogenous gene, e.g., many GPCRs where the in situ signal in the AMBA is undetectable.
evidence: This validates the Cre-driver line expression patterns against in situ hybridization data.

claim: Slc17a6Cre (Vglut2), which is expressed in most of the subclusters, reveals the overall distribution of glutamatergic projections from the PBN.
source: Slc17a6Cre (Vglut2), which is expressed in most of the subclusters, reveals the overall distribution of glutamatergic projections from the PBN (Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the use of a pan-glutamatergic Cre-driver line to map overall PBN projections, citing a reference.

claim: Cell populations in the PBN can be conceptually divided into two major groups based on overall projection patterns.
source: Cell populations in the PBN can be conceptually divided into two major groups based on overall projection patterns (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a summary statement about projection patterns, with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: The relatively dense projections from neurons in the PBle region generally follow the CTT.
source: The relatively dense projections from neurons in the PBle region generally follow the CTT, whereas the cells in the dorsal regions (PBld/ls/lc) follow the VP as described by Geerling and colleagues (Huang et al., 2021a, Huang et al., 2019; Karthik et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the projection pathway of PBle neurons, citing references.

claim: Cells in the dorsal regions (PBld/ls/lc) follow the VP.
source: The relatively dense projections from neurons in the PBle region generally follow the CTT, whereas the cells in the dorsal regions (PBld/ls/lc) follow the VP as described by Geerling and colleagues (Huang et al., 2021a, Huang et al., 2019; Karthik et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the projection pathway of dorsal PBN neurons, citing references.

claim: There is a smaller periventricular pathway that passes through the periaqueductal gray (PAG).
source: There is also a smaller periventricular pathway that passes through the periaqueductal gray (PAG, not shown) and a weak descending pathway to the hindbrain.
evidence: This describes an additional projection pathway from the PBN.

claim: There is a weak descending pathway to the hindbrain.
source: There is also a smaller periventricular pathway that passes through the periaqueductal gray (PAG, not shown) and a weak descending pathway to the hindbrain.
evidence: This describes another projection pathway from the PBN.

claim: None of the Cre-driver lines tested show projections exclusively along the periventricular or descending pathways.
source: None of the Cre-driver lines tested show projections exclusively along the periventricular or descending pathways.
evidence: This describes the projection patterns observed in the Cre-driver lines.

claim: Some PBN neurons, e.g., Tac1 neurons project along the descending pathway into the medulla and affect escape-like behaviors and breathing.
source: Some PBN neurons, e.g., Tac1 neurons project along the descending pathway into the medulla and affect escape-like behaviors and breathing (Arthurs et al. manuscript submitted; Barik et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the projection and function of Tac1 neurons, citing references.

claim: For Cre-driver lines that have most of their expression in the PBle, the axon terminals with the brightest signal are in the BNST and CEA.
source: For Cre-driver lines that have most of their expression in the PBle (Calca, Crhr1, Nts, Chat), or strongly in the PBle along with other regions (Crh, Adcyap1, Adcyap1r1, Tac1, Mc4r, Oprm1), the axon terminals with the brightest signal are in the BNST and CEA.
evidence: This describes the primary projection targets of PBle neurons.

claim: The oval and ventral regions of the BNST and the capsular region of the CEA have the strongest fluorescence from PBle projections.
source: Although expression is generally spread throughout these subregions, the oval and ventral regions of the BNST and the capsular region of the CEA have the strongest fluorescence.
evidence: This describes the specific subregions within BNST and CEA that receive the densest PBle projections.

claim: It is likely that the PBle cells are responsible for most of the oval/ventral BNST and capsular CEA staining density, while neurons outside of PBle project to adjacent regions.
source: It is likely that the PBle cells are responsible for most of the oval/ventral BNST and capsular CEA staining density, while neurons outside of PBle project to adjacent regions.
evidence: This is an inference about the source of projections to specific BNST and CEA subregions.

claim: The next brightest projection regions from PBle neurons are the IC, SI, VPMpc, and PSTN.
source: Although there is some variation, the next brightest regions are the IC, SI, VPMpc, and PSTN.
evidence: This describes secondary projection targets of PBle neurons.

claim: There are no lines with cell bodies in the PBle that do not have at least some synaptophysin signal in the BNST, CEA, IC, SI, VPMpc, and PSTN.
source: There are no lines with cell bodies in the PBle that do not have at least some synaptophysin signal in the above listed regions.
evidence: This describes the consistency of projection patterns from PBle neurons.

claim: Other areas that are often innervated by PBle neurons are the LS, CM, DMH, LHA, RE, IMD, PAG, DR, RN, and NTS.
source: Other areas that are often innervated are the LS, CM, DMH, LHA, RE, IMD, PAG, DR, RN, and NTS.
evidence: This describes additional projection targets of PBle neurons.

claim: Cre-driver lines that mainly have expression in the dorsal PBN regions (Pdyn, Tacr1, Brs3, Cbln4, Ptger3) have axons that tend to travel through and target ventral brain regions such as the VTA, LHA, DMH, PVH, and MEPO.
source: Cre-driver lines that mainly have expression in the dorsal PBN regions (Pdyn, Tacr1, Brs3, Cbln4, Ptger3) also have axons that tend to travel through and target ventral brain regions such as the VTA, LHA, DMH, PVH, and MEPO.
evidence: This describes the projection targets of dorsal PBN neurons.

claim: Cre-driver lines that are categorized into the dorsal group often have fewer cells and weaker projections.
source: Cre-driver lines that are categorized into the dorsal group often have fewer cells and weaker projections as a result.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of dorsal PBN Cre-driver lines.

claim: Some Cre-driver lines have strong cellular expression across most of the lateral PBN (Adcyap1, Adcyap1r1, Oprm1, Crh) and have robust expression in areas associated with both the CTT and VP.
source: Some Cre-driver lines have strong cellular expression across most of the lateral PBN. For these (Adcyap1, Adcyap1r1, Oprm1, Crh), there is robust expression of the AAV-driven fluorescent proteins in areas associated with the CTT such as the BNST/CEA and areas associated with the VP such as the MEPO.
evidence: This describes Cre-driver lines with broad expression and projections to both pathways.

claim: The cells that reside in the PBmm do not appear to have a separate innervation profile.
source: The cells that reside in the PBmm do not appear to have a separate innervation profile.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the projection patterns of PBmm neurons.

claim: There was no line examined that had its expression limited to the PBmm exclusively.
source: There was no line examined that had its expression limited to the PBmm exclusively.
evidence: This describes a limitation in the Cre-driver lines examined.

claim: Satb2-expressing neurons mainly reside in PBlv, scp, and PBmm.
source: The Satb2-expressing neurons mainly reside in PBlv, scp, and PBmm.
evidence: This describes the anatomical location of Satb2 neurons.

claim: Although Satb2 neurons are only partially expressed in PBle, their projection pathway still largely follows the CTT with connections to areas typically associated with PBle such as BNST and CEA.
source: Although they are only partially expressed in PBle, their projection pathway still largely follows the CTT with connections to areas typically associated with PBle such as BNST and CEA.
evidence: This describes the projection pattern of Satb2 neurons.

claim: Axon terminals from CalcaCre-driver line are concentrated in the oval BNST and lateral CEA, whereas Satb2Cre-driven projections surround those regions.
source: However, the axon terminals from CalcaCre-driver line are concentrated in the oval BNST and lateral CEA, whereas Satb2Cre-driven projections surround those regions (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: This describes the distinct projection patterns of Calca and Satb2 neurons within BNST and CEA, with reference to Figure 8.

claim: Ntsr1 population of neurons has the VMH as its most prominent projection target.
source: Ntsr1 population of neurons has the VMH as its most prominent projection target (Figure 8C).
evidence: This describes the primary projection target of Ntsr1 neurons, with reference to Figure 8C.

claim: A population of VMH-projecting PBN neurons was identified by Fulwiler and Saper, 1984; Fulwiler and Saper, 1985, who assigned it to the PBls subnucleus and found that about 80–90% of these neurons stained immunohistochemically for CCK.
source: A population of VMH-projecting PBN neurons was identified by Fulwiler and Saper, 1984; Fulwiler and Saper, 1985, who assigned it to the PBls subnucleus and found that about 80–90% of these neurons stained immunohistochemically for CCK.
evidence: This cites prior work that identified VMH-projecting PBN neurons.

claim: Ntsr1 neurons are a subpopulation of the Cck cells in the far rostral PBN.
source: Ntsr1 neurons are a subpopulation of the Cck cells in the far rostral PBN (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the relationship between Ntsr1 and Cck neurons, with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: All Cre-driver lines that have projections to the VMH (Crhr1, Nts, Adcyap1, Adcyap1r1, Oprm1) have some cell bodies in the same region as Ntsr1.
source: All Cre-driver lines that have projections to the VMH (Crhr1, Nts, Adcyap1, Adcyap1r1, Oprm1) have some cell bodies in the same region as Ntsr1.
evidence: This describes the anatomical overlap of VMH-projecting neurons.

claim: Many of the genes of interest are widely expressed in regions surrounding the PBN, which made restricting the transduction of cells within the PBN nearly impossible.
source: Many of the genes of interest are widely expressed in regions surrounding the PBN, which made restricting the transduction of cells within the PBN nearly impossible.
evidence: This describes a technical limitation of the viral tracing experiments.

claim: Gad2 and Slc32a1, the two GABAergic genes, are only sparsely expressed within the PBN compared to adjacent areas.
source: Gad2 and Slc32a1, the two GABAergic genes, are only sparsely expressed within the PBN compared to adjacent areas; consequently, we were unable to determine whether they function as interneurons or as projection neurons.
evidence: This describes the expression pattern of GABAergic markers and a limitation in determining their function.

claim: Gad2 is expressed more widely and without Slc32a1 in some PBN glutamatergic cells, e.g., Calca neurons.
source: Gad2 is expressed more widely and without Slc32a1 in some PBN glutamatergic cells, e.g., Calca neurons, so using that Cre-driver line to examine inhibitory projections outside of the PBN could be misleading.
evidence: This describes the expression pattern of Gad2 and a caution about using Gad2Cre mice.

claim: The results should facilitate more rigorous delineation of how specific PBN populations respond to and relay interoceptive and exteroceptive signals.
source: The results should facilitate more rigorous delineation of how specific PBN populations respond to and relay interoceptive and exteroceptive signals.
evidence: This is a statement about the expected impact of the study.

claim: The round tissue punches used to isolate the PBN included some adjacent regions.
source: As expected, the round tissue punches used to isolate the PBN included some adjacent regions; consequently, some of the UMAP clusters are not in the PBN.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the tissue collection method.

claim: Most of the PBN neurons express multiple neuropeptides and GPCR receptors.
source: Most of the PBN neurons express multiple neuropeptides and GPCR receptors; the co-expressed transcription factors likely play an important role in their cell-specific gene expression.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the molecular complexity of PBN neurons.

claim: The co-expressed transcription factors likely play an important role in cell-specific gene expression in PBN neurons.
source: Most of the PBN neurons express multiple neuropeptides and GPCR receptors; the co-expressed transcription factors likely play an important role in their cell-specific gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional role of transcription factors.

claim: Many of the neuropeptides expressed in the PBN were known to be expressed based on immunohistochemistry studies and confirmed by in situ hybridization.
source: Many of the neuropeptides expressed in the PBN, e.g., cholecystokinin, substance P, CGRP, somatostatin, prodynorphin, neurotensin, were known to be expressed in the PBN based on immunohistochemistry studies and confirmed by in situ hybridization (Hermanson et al., 1998; Saleh and Cechetto, 1996; Shimada et al., 1985)
evidence: This cites prior work that identified neuropeptide expression in the PBN.

claim: The overall axonal projections of the PBN neurons were established using anterograde tracers and confirmed using Slc17a6Cre mice and injections of AAV carrying Cre-dependent fluorescent genes.
source: The overall axonal projections of the PBN neurons were established using anterograde tracers and confirmed using Slc17a6Cre mice and injections of AAV carrying Cre-dependent fluorescent genes (Huang et al., 2021a).
evidence: This describes how overall PBN projections were characterized, citing a reference.

claim: The current data set provides a baseline for examining how the PBN changes during development and in response to environmental threats ranging from acute noxious events to chronic adverse conditions.
source: The current data set provides a baseline for examining how the PBN changes during development and in response to environmental threats ranging from acute noxious events to chronic adverse conditions.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential future applications of the dataset.

claim: The PBN has been divided into 10 subregions based on rigorous Nissl cytoarchitectural criteria.
source: The PBN has been divided into 10 subregions based on rigorous Nissl cytoarchitectural criteria; subsequent anterograde and retrograde tracing studies revealed relatively distinct projections to and from different subregions of the PBN (see references in Introduction).
evidence: This describes the historical anatomical characterization of the PBN.

claim: The nomenclature for different subregions of the PBN is not consistent in the literature.
source: As noted earlier, it is unfortunate that the nomenclature for different subregions of the PBN is not consistent in the literature, some regions are not shown at all in the AMBA, and a variety of abbreviations are used for the same subregions.
evidence: This is a comment on the inconsistency in PBN nomenclature across different sources.

claim: Gene expression patterns provide an additional means to define PBN subregions.
source: Gene expression patterns provide an additional means to define these subregions as shown in Figure 4.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of molecular markers for defining PBN anatomy.

claim: The results are consistent with those obtained by a new spatial-profiling method (PixelSeq) that was tested with PBN sections.
source: Our results are consistent with those obtained by a new spatial-profiling method (PixelSeq) that was tested with PBN sections (Fu et al., 2022).
evidence: This cites an independent study that validates the findings.

claim: mRNAs with prominent expression in each of the PBN subregions except the PBme were identified.
source: We identified mRNAs with prominent expression in each of the PBN subregions except the PBme.
evidence: This describes the coverage of the molecular characterization across PBN subregions.

claim: What was once considered to be a unique population turns out to be more complex, e.g., both the Calca and Pdyn neurons are represented by two clusters based on scRNA-Seq analysis.
source: Furthermore, what was once considered to be a unique population turns out to be more complex, e.g., both the Calca and Pdyn neurons are represented by two clusters based on scRNA-Seq analysis, and they could be subdivided even more by considering co-expression patterns of neuropeptides and other markers (Huang et al., 2021a, Huang et al., 2021b, Karthik et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the increased resolution of neuronal classification revealed by scRNA-Seq, citing references.

claim: Whether these closely related clusters have distinct projections and functions needs to be established.
source: Whether these closely related clusters have distinct projections and functions needs to be established, e.g., are distinct Pdyn neurons involved in conveying temperature, nocifensive behaviors, and feeding responses?
evidence: This is a statement about future research questions raised by the findings.

claim: The significance of the tight clustering of Calca neurons in rostral sections, with few if any interspersed neurons in the core of the PBle, is not known.
source: The significance of the tight clustering of Calca neurons in rostral sections, with few if any interspersed neurons in the core of the PBle, is not known; it is unlikely that gap junctions allow simultaneous activation because the activities of individual neurons expressing a fluorescent calcium indicator (GCaMP) are not synchronized (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about an unexplained observation, with a speculation about gap junctions ruled out by citing a reference.

claim: In contrast to the glutamatergic neurons, the GABAergic neurons are rare and dispersed throughout the PBN.
source: In contrast to the glutamatergic neurons, the GABAergic neurons are rare and dispersed throughout the PBN (Raver et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the distribution of GABAergic neurons, citing a reference.

claim: GABAergic neurons in the lateral PBN and caudal KF project axons to the brainstem.
source: GABAergic neurons in the lateral PBN and caudal KF project axons to the brainstem (Geerling et al., 2017; Yokota et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the projection pattern of GABAergic neurons, citing references.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of GABAergic neurons in the PBN region can inhibit the function of local glutamatergic neurons.
source: Chemogenetic activation of GABAergic neurons in the PBN region can inhibit the function of local glutamatergic neurons (Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes a functional role of GABAergic neurons, citing a reference.

claim: AAV-directed expression ChR2 in Slc32a1Cre neurons in the PBN region can inhibit CalcatdT neurons.
source: We have shown using electrophysiology that AAV-directed expression ChR2 in Slc32a1Cre neurons in the PBN region can inhibit CalcatdT neurons (Chen and Cao, unpublished).
evidence: This describes unpublished electrophysiology data showing GABAergic inhibition of Calca neurons.

claim: The choice of parameters used for clustering of scRNA-Seq data can affect the number of clusters.
source: The choice of parameters used for clustering of scRNA-Seq data can affect the number of clusters, and sequencing depth can influence the reliability of co-expression for low-abundance transcripts.
evidence: This is a statement about technical limitations of scRNA-Seq analysis.

claim: Sequencing depth can influence the reliability of co-expression for low-abundance transcripts.
source: The choice of parameters used for clustering of scRNA-Seq data can affect the number of clusters, and sequencing depth can influence the reliability of co-expression for low-abundance transcripts.
evidence: This is a statement about technical limitations of scRNA-Seq analysis.

claim: The number of cells in a neuronal subcluster expressing a particular GPCR mRNA (e.g., Oprm1) was low based on scRNA-Seq analysis, whereas the signal from the Oprm1Cre-driver line revealed many cells, suggesting that this mRNA was not detected in most of the cells that were sequenced.
source: For example, the number of cells in a neuronal subcluster expressing a particular GPCR mRNA (e.g., Oprm1) was low based on scRNA-Seq analysis, whereas the signal from the Oprm1Cre-driver line revealed many cells, suggesting that this mRNA was not detected in most to the cells that were sequenced.
evidence: This describes a discrepancy between scRNA-Seq and Cre-driver line expression, suggesting a detection limitation.

claim: ~100,000 reads/neuron may not have been enough to detect rare transcripts.
source: We obtained ~100,000 reads/neuron which may not have been enough to detect rare transcripts.
evidence: This is a statement about a potential limitation of the sequencing depth.

claim: A single mRNA/cell can maintain ~10,000 proteins with a half-life of 700 min at steady state.
source: A single mRNA/cell can maintain ~10,000 proteins with a half-life of 700 min at steady state (see 'Estimating mRNA and protein abundance per cell' in Materials and Methods), which may be enough for many regulatory proteins.
evidence: This is a calculation about the relationship between mRNA and protein abundance.

claim: Deeper sequencing of more neurons and using multiple distinguishing probes may reveal more cell types.
source: Deeper sequencing of more neurons and using multiple distinguishing probes may also reveal more cell types.
evidence: This is a speculation about how future studies could improve cell type identification.

claim: Defining and distinguishing between different neuron types are challenging, requiring identification of master transcription factors along with multiple kinds of analysis including functional studies.
source: Defining and distinguishing between different neuron types are challenging, requiring identification of master transcription factors along with multiple kinds of analysis including functional studies (Zeng, 2022).
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges of cell type classification, citing a reference.

claim: The results reported here will undoubtedly be refined by further investigation.
source: Thus, the results reported here will undoubtedly be refined by further investigation.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging that the findings are subject to refinement.

claim: Mice of both sexes were pooled for scRNA-Seq experiment, and only male mice were used for the HiPlex experiment.
source: Mice of both sexes were pooled for scRNA-Seq experiment, and only male mice were used for the HiPlex experiment, so future studies should consider this variable.
evidence: This describes a limitation regarding sex as a biological variable.

claim: There was good, low-resolution correspondence among HiPlex, AMBA, and fluorescent protein expression from Cre-driver lines when transcripts were abundant.
source: Nevertheless, there was good, low-resolution correspondence among HiPlex, AMBA, and fluorescent protein expression from Cre-driver lines when transcripts were abundant, but we failed to detect a signal for some HiPlex probes (Fn1, Mylk, Slc35d3, Shisal2b) that were distinguishing genes based on scRNA-Seq analysis.
evidence: This describes the validation of scRNA-Seq findings with in situ hybridization and Cre-driver lines, noting some failures.

claim: Some HiPlex probes (Fn1, Mylk, Slc35d3, Shisal2b) that were distinguishing genes based on scRNA-Seq analysis failed to produce a detectable signal.
source: Nevertheless, there was good, low-resolution correspondence among HiPlex, AMBA, and fluorescent protein expression from Cre-driver lines when transcripts were abundant, but we failed to detect a signal for some HiPlex probes (Fn1, Mylk, Slc35d3, Shisal2b) that were distinguishing genes based on scRNA-Seq analysis.
evidence: This describes a limitation where some predicted markers could not be validated by in situ hybridization.

claim: There were cases where predictions were not supported by HiPlex analysis (e.g., N5, N6, N18) even though scRNA-Seq indicated that these clusters express many of the same distinguishing transcription factors as other PBN clusters.
source: There were also cases where predictions were not supported by HiPlex analysis (e.g., N5, N6, N18) even though scRNA-Seq indicated that these clusters express many of the same distinguishing transcription factors as other PBN clusters.
evidence: This describes cases where subclusters could not be anatomically localized despite molecular characterization.

claim: Cre-driver lines are helpful for locating some neurons with low levels of gene expression (e.g., Ntsr1, Avpr1a) because the action of a few Cre recombinase molecules is sufficient to activate robust expression from AAV carrying a Cre-dependent gene.
source: Cre-driver lines are helpful for locating some neurons with low levels of gene expression (e.g., Ntsr1, Avpr1a) because, in principle, the action of a few Cre recombinase molecules is sufficient to activate robust expression from AAV carrying a Cre-dependent gene.
evidence: This describes an advantage of using Cre-driver lines for detecting low-abundance gene expression.

claim: When genes are expressed in the PBN as well as neighboring regions (e.g., Slc32a1, Phox2b), restricting AAV transduction to the PBN is challenging.
source: When genes are expressed in the PBN as well as neighboring regions (e.g., Slc32a1, Phox2b), restricting AAV transduction to the PBN is challenging.
evidence: This describes a technical limitation of viral tracing experiments.

claim: It is difficult to assure that any viral injection transduces all the relevant neurons within the PBN without doing an exhaustive analysis of each line.
source: It is also difficult to assure that any viral injection transduces all the relevant neurons within the PBN without doing an exhaustive analysis of each line.
evidence: This describes a limitation in ensuring complete transduction of target neurons.

claim: Animals and tissue sections were processed at different times, so variations in brightness could be due to aspects such as perfusion or staining quality rather than expression differences.
source: Animals and tissue sections were processed at different times, so variations in brightness could be due to aspects such as perfusion or staining quality rather than expression differences.
evidence: This describes a potential source of variability in the imaging data.

claim: The five coronal sections used for the HiPlex experiments did not include the most rostral region of the PBN, which explains the difficulty in locating clusters N4 and N9.
source: The five coronal sections used for the HiPlex experiments did not include the most rostral region of the PBN, which explains our difficulty in locating clusters N4 and N9.
evidence: This describes a limitation in the anatomical coverage of the HiPlex experiments.

claim: Probes for some genes known to be expressed in the PBN and detected by scRNA-Seq (e.g., Penk, Grp, Nmb, Mc4r) were not included in the HiPlex experiments.
source: We did not include probes for some genes that are known to be expressed in the PBN and detected by scRNA-Seq (Table 1), e.g., Penk (Engström et al., 2001), Grp (Karthik et al., 2022), Nmb (Huang et al., 2022), and Mc4r (Paues et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes genes that were not examined by in situ hybridization despite being detected by scRNA-Seq.

claim: It will be important to determine whether any of the genes not examined by HiPlex are co-localized with the in situ probes that were used.
source: It will be important to determine whether any of them are co-localized with the in situ probes that we used.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Numerous studies with CalcaCre, PdynCre, and Tacr1Cre mice have revealed their activation by a wide variety of real and potential threats.
source: For example, numerous studies with CalcaCre,PdynCre, and Tacr1Cre mice have revealed their activation by a wide variety of real and potential threats, while their optogenetic or chemogenetic activation is generally aversive, and their inactivation ameliorates aversive responses to threats (references are included in Results, under N10, N15, N17).
evidence: This summarizes findings from multiple studies using specific Cre-driver lines.

claim: Optogenetic or chemogenetic activation of CalcaCre, PdynCre, and Tacr1Cre neurons is generally aversive.
source: For example, numerous studies with CalcaCre,PdynCre, and Tacr1Cre mice have revealed their activation by a wide variety of real and potential threats, while their optogenetic or chemogenetic activation is generally aversive, and their inactivation ameliorates aversive responses to threats (references are included in Results, under N10, N15, N17).
evidence: This summarizes findings from manipulation studies.

claim: Inactivation of CalcaCre, PdynCre, and Tacr1Cre neurons ameliorates aversive responses to threats.
source: For example, numerous studies with CalcaCre,PdynCre, and Tacr1Cre mice have revealed their activation by a wide variety of real and potential threats, while their optogenetic or chemogenetic activation is generally aversive, and their inactivation ameliorates aversive responses to threats (references are included in Results, under N10, N15, N17).
evidence: This summarizes findings from inactivation studies.

claim: An alternative strategy uses Cre-driver mice with widespread expression in the PBN (e.g., Slc17a6Cre, CckCre, Oprm1Cre, and Tac1Cre) to assess behavioral and physiological consequences of their activation or inhibition.
source: An alternative strategy uses Cre-driver mice with widespread expression in the PBN, e.g., Slc17a6Cre, CckCre, Oprm1Cre, and Tac1Cre, to assess behavioral and physiological consequences of their activation or inhibition (Barik et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2020; Chiang et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes an alternative experimental approach using broadly expressed Cre-driver lines, citing references.

claim: A problem with Cre-driver lines with widespread PBN expression is the difficulty in restricting viral transduction to the PBN.
source: A problem with these Cre-drivers is the difficulty in restricting viral transduction to the PBN.
evidence: This describes a limitation of using broadly expressed Cre-driver lines.

claim: Both restricted and widespread Cre-driver approaches have flaws because it is rare for threats to activate only one cell type, and all the cells represented by the more widely expressed genes are rarely engaged by specific threats.
source: Both approaches have flaws because it is rare for threats to activate only one cell type, and all the cells represented by the more widely expressed genes are rarely engaged by specific threats.
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of the limitations of Cre-driver line approaches.

claim: Activation of some PBN neurons can suppress the activity of others, e.g., activation of Tac1 neurons counteracts the outcomes of activating Calca neurons even though Tac1 and Calca are co-expressed in the PBle.
source: Furthermore, activation of some PBN neurons can suppress the activity of others, e.g., activation of Tac1 neurons counteracts the outcomes of activating Calca neurons even though Tac1 and Calca are co-expressed in the PBle (Arthurs et al. manuscript submitted).
evidence: This describes an interaction between PBN neuron populations, citing a manuscript in submission.

claim: The possibility that activation of some PBN neurons can suppress others complicates interpretation of results when groups of neurons are artificially manipulated.
source: This possibility complicates interpretation of results when groups of neurons are artificially manipulated.
evidence: This is an inference about the challenges of interpreting manipulation experiments.

claim: One solution to the problem of artificial manipulation is tagging and manipulating groups of neurons that are normally engaged by specific threats, e.g., using FosTrap techniques.
source: One solution to this problem is tagging and manipulating groups of neurons that are normally engaged by specific threats, e.g., FosTrap (DeNardo and Luo, 2017; Sakurai et al., 2016) techniques have been used to identify PBN neurons activated by pain or aversive odors (Liu et al., 2022; Rodriguez et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes an alternative experimental approach using activity-dependent labeling, citing references.

claim: The broad outlines of axonal projections from the PBN were established decades ago by anterograde tracing studies and confirmed by injection of AAV-expressing Cre-dependent fluorescent markers in the PBN of Slc17a6Cre mice.
source: The broad outlines of axonal projections from the PBN were established decades ago by anterograde tracing studies (Fulwiler and Saper, 1984; Gauriau and Bernard, 2002; Krout and Loewy, 2000; Moga et al., 1990; Norgren and Leonard, 1971; Tokita et al., 2009) and confirmed by injection of AAV-expressing Cre-dependent fluorescent markers in the PBN of Slc17a6Cre mice (Chiang et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2021a).
evidence: This summarizes the historical and recent characterization of PBN projections, citing multiple references.

claim: The axonal tracts to the forebrain follow two main paths as they leave the PBN: the CTT pathway and the VP.
source: The axonal tracts to the forebrain follow two main paths as they leave the PBN. The CTT pathway travels to the forebrain via the ventral thalamus, to the extended amygdala and cerebral cortex. The VP travels through the ventral tegmental area to the hypothalamus.
evidence: This describes the two major ascending pathways from the PBN.

claim: The CTT pathway travels to the forebrain via the ventral thalamus, to the extended amygdala and cerebral cortex.
source: The CTT pathway travels to the forebrain via the ventral thalamus, to the extended amygdala and cerebral cortex.
evidence: This describes the trajectory of the CTT pathway.

claim: The VP travels through the ventral tegmental area to the hypothalamus.
